1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement

Density Functional Theory (DFT) is the workhorse of computational chemistry, but the iterative Self-Consistent Field (SCF) method required to solve the Kohn-Sham equations scales poorly with system size (typically cubic or quartic scaling). While Deep Learning has shown promise in predicting the Hamiltonian matrix directly—bypassing the SCF loop—current approaches face a critical scalability barrier when applied to large molecular systems.

We observe a phenomenon where models trained on small molecules fail to generalize to larger ones, even when the element-wise error of the predicted Hamiltonian matrix remains low. This discrepancy arises because the mapping from Hamiltonian matrix entries to physical properties (eigenvalues/energies) becomes increasingly sensitive to perturbations as the system size and basis set size grow. In large systems, the overlap matrix becomes ill-conditioned, amplifying small prediction errors into catastrophic inaccuracies for physical properties like total energy and band gaps. Standard loss functions (MSE/MAE) are insufficient because they treat the Hamiltonian as a grid of numbers rather than an operator defining a quantum state.

## Core Hypothesis

We hypothesize that to achieve physical accuracy and scalability for large molecules, we must constrain the learning process using spectral information rather than relying solely on element-wise matrix reconstruction.

Our core intuition is that a correct Hamiltonian must preserve the eigenspace of the ground truth system. We propose that by explicitly aligning the *action* of the predicted Hamiltonian with the wavefunctions (eigenvectors) of the ground truth, we can force the network to learn physically meaningful representations. Furthermore, we hypothesize that the computational cost of equivariant networks for large systems can be mitigated by combining efficient rotation-aligned convolutions with a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture that decouples short-range and long-range interaction dynamics.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a dual-pronged strategy focusing on a physics-informed loss function and a scalable network architecture.

**1. Wavefunction Alignment Strategy (The Supervisory Signal)**
Instead of relying only on direct regression of Hamiltonian matrix elements, we will introduce a spectral alignment objective.
*   **Intuition:** We will utilize the ground-truth eigenvectors (coefficients) as a fixed basis. We will project our *predicted* Hamiltonian onto this basis. If the prediction is physically accurate, this projection should yield a diagonal matrix containing the correct orbital energies.
*   **Avoidance of Eigensolvers:** Crucially, we will *not* perform eigendecomposition on the predicted matrix during training, as backpropagating through eigensolvers is numerically unstable and expensive. Instead, we use the ground-truth eigenvectors (which are constant during training) to "probe" the quality of the predicted Hamiltonian.
*   **Orbital Reweighting:** Recognizing that chemical properties are dominated by occupied orbitals and the lowest unoccupied orbital (LUMO), we will apply a weighting scheme that penalizes errors in these chemically relevant subspaces significantly more than errors in high-energy virtual orbitals.

**2. Scalable Network Architecture (The Model)**
To handle the complexity of large molecular graphs without prohibitive computational costs, we will design a specialized equivariant network.
*   **Efficient Equivariance:** We will replace standard SO(3) tensor product convolutions with a more efficient variant that aligns interactions to a canonical axis (effectively reducing operations to 2D rotations). This allows us to use higher-degree spherical tensors—essential for modeling complex orbitals—without the cubic complexity scaling usually associated with them.
*   **Distance-Aware Mixture of Experts:** We will implement a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism for pairwise interactions. The logic here is that the physics of local chemical bonds differs fundamentally from long-range electrostatic interactions. A gating network will route atom pairs to specific "expert" modules based on spatial distance, allowing the model to learn specialized functions for different interaction regimes while maintaining sparsity.
*   **Many-Body Interaction Head:** For the diagonal blocks of the Hamiltonian (self-interactions), we will employ a many-body interaction layer that constructs high-order features from lower-order representations, ensuring we capture complex electron correlation effects inherent in larger systems.

## Expected Contribution

This research expects to bridge the gap between deep learning and practical, large-scale quantum chemistry.
1.  **Theoretical:** We aim to demonstrate that spectral alignment is a necessary condition for learning extensive properties in large quantum systems, effectively solving the "matrix-accuracy vs. physical-accuracy" divergence.
2.  **Practical:** We anticipate delivering a model capable of predicting Hamiltonians for molecules with 40-100+ atoms with high physical fidelity. This will enable two key outcomes:
    *   **Direct Property Prediction:** Accurate estimation of HOMO-LUMO gaps and total energies without solving the Schrödinger equation.
    *   **SCF Acceleration:** Providing high-quality initial guesses that drastically reduce (or eliminate) the number of iterations required for convergence in traditional DFT solvers.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive experimental framework to evaluate the scalability and applicability of deep-learning models for predicting Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians, specifically focusing on large molecular systems.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **PubChemQH (New Contribution):** Generated from PubChemQC. Contains molecules with molecular weight > 400.
        *   **Size:** 50,321 molecules (Total).
        *   **Splits:** 40,257 Training, 5,032 Validation, 5,032 Test.
        *   **Atom Count:** 40 to 100 atoms per molecule (Mean: 61.85).
        *   **Configuration:** B3LYP functional, Def2TZVP basis set.
        *   **Ground Truth Generation:** CUDA-accelerated SCF implementation (128 NVIDIA-V100 GPUs for ~1 month).
    *   **QH9:** Based on QM9 (stable geometries).
        *   **Size:** 130,831 molecules.
        *   **Atom Count:** Up to 9 heavy atoms (Mean: 18).
        *   **Configuration:** B3LYP functional, Def2SVP basis set.
        *   **Variations:** Evaluated on both QH9-stable and QH9-dynamic configurations.
    *   **Elongated Alkanes ($C_xH_{2x+2}$):** Used for out-of-distribution scalability testing. Atom counts up to 182.

*   **Models Compared:**
    *   **WANet (Proposed):** Evaluated with and without Wavefunction Alignment Loss (WALoss).
    *   **QHNet:** Evaluated with and without WALoss.
    *   **PhisNet:** Evaluated with WALoss.
    *   **Initial Guess:** Minneapolish Atomic Orbitals (minao) / Fock matrix initialization.
    *   **Property Regression Baselines (Invariant Heads):** Equiformer V2, UniMol+, UniMol2, EGNN, ViSNet.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Hamiltonian Accuracy:** Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of Hamiltonian matrix elements.
    *   **Orbital Energies (kcal/mol):** MAE for $\epsilon_{HOMO}$, $\epsilon_{LUMO}$, $\epsilon_{\Delta}$ (HOMO-LUMO gap), $\epsilon_{occ}$ (occupied orbitals), $\epsilon_{orb}$ (all orbitals).
    *   **System Energy:** MAE of total system energy derived from the Hamiltonian via pyscf (kcal/mol).
    *   **Wavefunction Quality:** Cosine Similarity of eigenvectors ($C$).
    *   **Computational Efficiency:** Relative SCF iterations (compared to initial guess), Inference speed (it/s), Peak GPU Memory (GB).
    *   **Additional Properties:** Dipole Moment MAE (Debye), Electronic Spatial Extent MAE (a.u.).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Framework:** PyTorch / PyG.
    *   **Loss Function:** Combination of MSE/MAE on Hamiltonian elements + WALoss (Wavefunction Alignment Loss).
    *   **Optimization:** Adam optimizer.
    *   **Learning Rate:** 0.001 (PubChemQH), 5e-4 (QH9). Polynomial scheduler with 1,000 warmup steps.
    *   **Batch Size:** 8 (PubChemQH), 32 (QH9).
    *   **Training Duration:** Max 300,000 steps with early stopping (patience 1,000).
    *   **Hardware:** Training and inference evaluation performed on NVIDIA GPUs (V100/A100 implied by context of large scale).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Observation on SAD Phenomenon:** We identified a "Scaling-Induced MAE-Applicability Divergence" (SAD). While small molecules yield accurate system energies with Hamiltonian relative MAEs up to 200%, large molecules show energy errors up to 1,000,000 kcal/mol at only 0.01% relative MAE.
*   **Observation on Learning Instability:** The learning curve analysis revealed that minimizing elementwise Hamiltonian loss alone leads to significant fluctuations in system energy; a Hamiltonian MAE of ~0.3 resulted in system energy MAE spikes up to 30,000 kcal/mol.
*   **Observation on WANet Efficiency:** WANet demonstrated superior efficiency compared to QHNet. Specifically, WANet required 39.22 hours for training versus 90.43 hours for QHNet. Peak GPU memory usage was lower for WANet (15.86 GB) compared to QHNet (26.49 GB). Inference speed was faster for WANet (1.09 it/s) compared to QHNet (0.45 it/s).
*   **Observation on SCF Acceleration:** The WANet-augmented SCF method reduced the relative SCF iterations to 82%, whereas models without WALoss (QHNet, WANet) increased iterations to >300%, and the Initial Guess stood at 100%. This translates to faster wall-clock time for density functional theory calculations.
*   **Observation on Scalability (Alkanes):** In experiments with elongated alkanes ($C_xH_{2x+2}$), models without WALoss showed rapid error degradation as atom count increased into the "D2" (out-of-distribution) region. WANet with WALoss maintained low MAE for HOMO and LUMO predictions even for molecules with up to 182 atoms.
*   **Observation on Eigenvalue Scaling:** We observed that the reciprocal of the minimum eigenvalue of the overlap matrix ($1/\lambda_{min}$) scales linearly with the number of carbon atoms in saturated hydrocarbons. In other systems (e.g., Diamond, Graphene), it follows a power law relationship with the number of basis functions.
*   **Observation on Condition Number:** Molecules in the PubChemQH dataset exhibited substantially higher condition number ratios ($\frac{\kappa(\mathbf{S})}{\|\mathbf{S}\|_2}$) compared to the QH9 dataset, indicating higher perturbation sensitivity in larger systems.
*   **Observation on Property Regression:** While WANet with WALoss outperformed property regression models (e.g., Equiformer V2) on HOMO/LUMO/Gap accuracy, property regression models struggled to generalize to saturated carbon systems not included in the training set. WANet with WALoss closely replicated ground truth energy levels for C20H42.
*   **Observation on Architectural Components:** The ablation study confirmed that removing the SO(2) convolution significantly increased memory usage (13.87GB vs 24.47GB) and reduced inference speed (1.34 it/s vs 0.51 it/s). The Many-Body and LSR-MoE components were essential for achieving the lowest Hamiltonian and orbital energy MAEs.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Density Functional Theory (DFT) is the standard for investigating electronic structure in chemistry and materials science. However, the construction of the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian matrix is computationally expensive, scaling as $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ or $\mathcal{O}(N^4)$ with respect to the number of electrons. While Deep Learning (DL) models—specifically SE(3)-equivariant neural networks—have been proposed to predict Hamiltonians directly from atomic configurations, they face a critical scalability barrier when applied to large molecular systems (e.g., 40–100 atoms).

We identify a phenomenon we term **Scaling-Induced MAE-Applicability Divergence (SAD)**. In large systems, a low Mean Absolute Error (MAE) in the predicted Hamiltonian elements does not guarantee physical validity. Due to the ill-conditioning of the overlap matrix $\mathbf{S}$ in large basis sets, small element-wise perturbations in the Hamiltonian $\hat{\mathbf{H}}$ lead to catastrophic errors in the resulting eigenvalues (orbital energies) and total system energy. Existing loss functions (MSE/MAE) fail to constrain the eigenstructure of the Hamiltonian, rendering predictions for large molecules physically useless. Furthermore, current equivariant architectures (like Tensor Field Networks) are computationally too heavy ($\mathcal{O}(L^6)$ complexity for tensor products) to scale effectively to the high-degree representations required for these systems.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose a two-pronged solution to solve the scalability and applicability crisis in Hamiltonian learning:

1.  **Physically-Informed Loss Landscape:** We hypothesize that we can bypass the instability of backpropagating through eigensolvers by introducing **Wavefunction Alignment Loss (WALoss)**. By using ground-truth eigenvectors as a fixed basis to project the predicted Hamiltonian, we can enforce alignment of the eigenspaces and penalize orbital energy errors directly, implicitely accounting for the condition number of the overlap matrix.
2.  **Scalable Architecture (WANet):** We propose **WANet**, a localized equivariant network that replaces expensive SO(3) convolutions with efficient SO(2) operations (via eSCN) and introduces a **Sparse Mixture of Pair Experts**. This will allow the model to capture both long-range electrostatics and short-range quantum interactions efficiently without the prohibitive computational cost of fully connected tensor products.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a unified framework consisting of a modernized equivariant network (WANet) trained via a spectral-aware objective function (WALoss).

### 1. Wavefunction Alignment Loss (WALoss) formulation

To mitigate the SAD phenomenon, we must constrain the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the predicted Hamiltonian $\hat{\mathbf{H}}$. Direct backpropagation through the generalized eigenvalue problem $\hat{\mathbf{H}}\hat{\mathbf{C}} = \mathbf{S}\hat{\mathbf{C}}\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}$ is numerically unstable.

Instead, we will exploit the orthogonality of the ground-truth eigenvectors $\mathbf{C}^\star$ with respect to the overlap matrix $\mathbf{S}$. We propose a loss function that performs a basis change on the *predicted* Hamiltonian to align it with the observed one.

Let $\mathbf{H}^\star$ be the ground truth Hamiltonian, satisfying $\mathbf{H}^\star \mathbf{C}^\star = \mathbf{S} \mathbf{C}^\star \boldsymbol{\epsilon}^\star$. We define the Wavefunction Alignment Loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WA}}$ as:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WA}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left\lVert (\mathbf{C}_{(i)}^\star)^\top \hat{\mathbf{H}}_{(i)} \mathbf{C}_{(i)}^\star - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{(i)}^\star \right\rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^2
$$

where $n$ is the batch size, $\hat{\mathbf{H}}$ is the predicted Hamiltonian, and $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^\star$ is the diagonal matrix of ground-truth orbital energies. This formulation penalizes off-diagonal elements in the transformed basis (enforcing correct eigenvectors) and diagonal elements (enforcing correct eigenvalues) simultaneously.

**Reweighting Strategy:**
Recognizing that occupied orbitals and the Lowest Unoccupied Molecular Orbital (LUMO) determine chemical properties, we will introduce a weighted variant. Let $\mathcal{I}$ be the set of indices for occupied orbitals plus the LUMO. We formulate the weighted loss as:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{weighted}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \rho \sum_{j \in \mathcal{I}} \Delta_{ij} + \xi \sum_{j \notin \mathcal{I}} \Delta_{ij} \right)
$$

where $\Delta_{ij} = \lVert (\mathbf{C}_{(i)}^\star)_j^\top \hat{\mathbf{H}}_{(i)} (\mathbf{C}_{(i)}^\star)_j - (\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{(i)}^\star)_j \rVert_{\mathrm{F}}^2$, and $\rho \gg \xi$ are hyperparameters to prioritize chemically relevant states.

### 2. WANet Architecture Design

The architecture will consist of two primary modules: a Node Convolution Layer for feature extraction and a Hamiltonian Head for matrix construction.

**A. Node Convolution via eSCN (SO(2) Reduction)**
To handle high-degree spherical tensors efficiently, we will replace standard SO(3) convolutions with Equivariant Spherical Channel Networks (eSCN). We will rotate the input features $x_s$ and relative position $\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{ts}$ such that $\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{ts}$ aligns with the y-axis. This reduces the symmetry group to SO(2), simplifying the tensor product computation from $\mathcal{O}(L^6)$ to $\mathcal{O}(L^3)$.

The message passing operation will be defined as:
$$
m_{ts}^{(\ell_o)} = (D^{(\ell_o)})^{-1} \sum_{\ell_i} \bigoplus_{m_o} (y_{ts}^{\ell_i, \ell_o})_{m_o}
$$
where $D$ is the Wigner-D matrix for rotation, and $y_{ts}$ represents the efficiently computed point-wise convolution in the rotated frame.

**B. Hamiltonian Head: Sparse Mixture of Long-Short-Range Experts**
Molecular interactions vary significantly with distance. We will implement a Gated Mixture-of-Experts (GMoE) layer to differentiate between proximal (covalent) and distal (non-covalent) interactions.

The output for a pair of atoms $(t, s)$ will be:
$$
F_{\mathrm{MoE}}(x_t, x_s) = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{exp}} p_k(x_t, x_s) \cdot F_{\mathrm{pair}}^k(x_t, x_s)
$$
where $N_{exp}$ is the number of experts. The gating probabilities $p_k$ are computed via a Gumbel-Softmax mechanism over radial basis function inputs $z = \mathrm{rbf}(\|\mathbf{r}_{ts}\|_2)$:
$$
p_k(x_t, x_s) = \frac{\exp(G_k(z) + \eta_k)}{\sum_{m} \exp(G_m(z) + \eta_m)}
$$
Here, $G_k(z)$ is a learned gating score and $\eta_k$ is Gumbel noise to ensure load balancing and exploration. Each expert $F_{\mathrm{pair}}^k$ effectively learns a distinct tensor product interaction profile suitable for a specific distance regime.

**C. Diagonal Block Construction (Many-Body Interactions)**
For the diagonal blocks of the Hamiltonian (self-interactions), we must capture electron correlation effects beyond pairwise approximations. We will employ a "density trick" similar to the MACE framework. We will form generalized higher-order features $B_{M, \nu}^{L}$ by combining lower-order features:

$$
B_{M, \nu}^{L} = \sum_{lm} C_{lm, \nu}^{LM} \prod_{\xi=1}^{\nu} w_{l_\xi} f_{m}^{l}
$$

This allows the network to implicitly model $\nu$-body interactions, crucial for accurate diagonal term prediction.

### 3. Training Protocol
The model will be trained to minimize a composite loss function combining the standard Frobenius norm of the Hamiltonian difference and our proposed Wavefunction Alignment Loss:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{MSE}} \|\hat{\mathbf{H}} - \mathbf{H}^\star\|_F^2 + \lambda_{\mathrm{WA}} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WA}}
$$

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Theoretical Advancement:** We expect to demonstrate that element-wise supervision is insufficient for Hamiltonian learning in large bases due to the overlap matrix condition number. The WALoss will provide a theoretically grounded method to inject physical constraints (eigenspectrum validity) into the learning process without the cost of eigendecomposition during training.
2.  **Scalability:** By integrating eSCN and Mixture-of-Experts, WANet will significantly reduce the memory and computational footprint required to reach high-angular-momentum features, enabling the modeling of systems with 40-100+ atoms.
3.  **Applicability:** The proposed framework is expected to produce Hamiltonians that yield physically accurate derived properties (HOMO/LUMO gaps, total energies) and serve as high-quality initial guesses to accelerate traditional Self-Consistent Field (SCF) iterations.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no coding agent: a 23-stage prompt-chain pipeline over the Anthropic Messages API

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
